abstract: This comprehensive survey by Fossen, McLemore, and Sorgner reviews the emerging literature on AI's impact on entrepreneurship, drawing on both theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence. Using original survey data from the German Socio-economic Panel, the authors find that entrepreneurs, particularly those with employees, are aware of and use AI technologies significantly more frequently than paid employees. The paper distinguishes between two pathways through which AI affects entrepreneurship: AI technologies that automate jobs tend to increase necessity entrepreneurship (displaced workers turning to self-employment), while AI technologies that transform jobs without fully displacing workers increase opportunity entrepreneurship (new ventures enabled by AI capabilities). The survey covers AI's effects on entrepreneurial opportunities, decision-making under uncertainty, startup entry barriers, entrepreneurial performance, and regional entrepreneurship ecosystems. The authors also examine how EU AI regulation may shape the entrepreneurship landscape by creating compliance burdens that disproportionately affect small ventures.
keyFindings: Entrepreneurs with employees are aware of and use AI technologies significantly more frequently than paid employees, based on German Socio-economic Panel data.

AI that automates jobs increases necessity entrepreneurship (displaced workers pushed into self-employment), while AI that transforms jobs increases opportunity entrepreneurship (new ventures enabled by AI).

AI impacts regional entrepreneurship ecosystems by altering the importance of existing ecosystem elements, creating new ones, and potentially reducing the role of geography in entrepreneurial success.
EU AI regulation may create compliance burdens that disproportionately affect small ventures and startups, potentially tilting the competitive landscape toward larger, better-resourced firms.

The distinction between job-automating and job-transforming AI is critical for predicting whether AI-driven entrepreneurship will be primarily necessity-driven (a negative signal) or opportunity-driven (a positive signal).
methodology: Literature survey and original empirical analysis. The survey component reviews the theoretical and empirical literature on AI and entrepreneurship across multiple dimensions (opportunities, decision-making, entry barriers, performance, ecosystems, regulation). The empirical component uses German Socio-economic Panel (SOEP) survey data to analyze AI awareness and usage patterns among entrepreneurs vs. employees. Published as IZA Discussion Paper No. 17055, June 2024.
qualifiers: The empirical evidence is drawn from the German context and may not generalize to other economies with different entrepreneurship cultures or regulatory environments. The literature on AI and entrepreneurship is young, with most studies correlational rather than causal. The distinction between necessity and opportunity entrepreneurship is conceptually clean but empirically difficult to measure. Survey-based AI usage data may reflect definitional inconsistencies. The discussion paper has not yet undergone formal peer review.
